roles.title: Data Engineer
roles.summary: Builds and runs the pipelines, models and warehouses that data products stand on.

roles.title: Analytics Engineer
roles.summary: Turns raw data into tested, documented models that analysts and dashboards can trust.

roles.title: Data Platform Engineer
roles.summary: Builds the shared data platform other teams build on: storage, compute, orchestration, governance.

roles.title: Machine Learning Engineer
roles.summary: Trains, ships and operates machine learning models in production.

roles.title: AI Engineer
roles.summary: Builds products on large language models: retrieval, agents, evaluation, cost and latency.

roles.title: Data Scientist
roles.summary: Answers product and business questions with statistics, experiments and models.

roles.title: Associate Product Manager
roles.summary: Early-career PM: owns a well-scoped area, learns to frame problems, ship and measure.

roles.title: Group Product Manager
roles.summary: Leads a group of PMs and a portfolio of products; accountable for outcomes through other people.

roles.title: Principal Product Manager
roles.summary: Senior individual contributor who sets direction across teams for the hardest, most ambiguous problems.

roles.title: Director of Product Management
roles.summary: Runs a product organisation: strategy, structure, hiring, operating rhythm and results.

roles.title: LLM / Agentic AI Product Manager
roles.summary: Builds products where language models plan and act: agents, tools, autonomy and the guardrails around them.

roles.title: AI Platform Product Manager
roles.summary: Builds the platform other teams build AI on: model access, evaluation tooling, serving, governance.

roles.title: Generative AI Product Manager
roles.summary: Ships user-facing generative AI features: assistants, copilots and content generation.

roles.title: Machine Learning Product Manager
roles.summary: Owns products powered by predictive models: ranking, recommendations, fraud, forecasting.

roles.title: AI Product Manager
roles.summary: Generalist AI PM: finds where AI earns its keep, ships it responsibly and proves the value.

roles.title: AI Technical Program Manager
roles.summary: Runs programs that ship models and AI systems: compute, data, evaluation and launch gates.

roles.title: Cloud / Infrastructure Program Manager
roles.summary: Runs infrastructure programs: capacity, migrations, data centres, reliability and cost.

roles.title: Senior Technical Program Manager
roles.summary: Leads multi-team, multi-quarter programs with ambiguous scope and executive visibility.

roles.title: Technical Program Manager
roles.summary: Drives cross-team engineering programs to delivery: plans, dependencies, risks and decisions.

roles.title: Engineering Program Manager
roles.summary: Runs engineering execution for a product area: release trains, quality gates and cross-team delivery.

roles.title: Technical Product Manager
roles.summary: Product manager for technical products — APIs, SDKs, platforms and developer tools. Owns WHAT and WHY, not the program plan.

roles.title: Data Product Manager
roles.summary: Treats data as a product: datasets, data platforms and metrics other teams rely on.

roles.title: Platform Product Manager
roles.summary: Builds internal or external platforms whose customers are other teams and developers.

roles.title: Data / BI Analyst
roles.summary: Builds the reports, dashboards and analyses the business runs on.

roles.title: Product Analyst
roles.summary: Answers product questions with data: metrics, funnels, experiments and root-cause analysis.

roles.title: Growth Product Manager
roles.summary: Moves acquisition, activation, retention and monetisation through fast, measured experiments.

roles.title: Product Marketing Manager
roles.summary: Owns positioning, messaging and launches: why this product, for whom, and how the market hears it.

roles.title: Product Operations Manager
roles.summary: Builds the operating system of a product org: rituals, tooling, insights and launch process.

roles.title: Product Strategy Manager
roles.summary: Shapes where the product org plays: markets, bets, business cases and portfolio choices.

roles.title: Senior Product Manager
roles.summary: Owns a product area end to end, sets its strategy and leads through ambiguity without formal authority.

roles.title: Product Manager
roles.summary: Owns outcomes for a product area: what to build, why, for whom, and whether it worked.

categories.title: Product Sense
categories.summary: Can you find a real user problem worth solving and shape a product that solves it?
steps: Clarify the goal and the constraint (business goal, platform, time).
Choose one user segment on purpose and say why.
List that segment's pain points; pick the most important.
Generate a few distinct solutions; choose one with explicit criteria.
Define success and the first version you would ship.
pitfalls: Jumping to features before the problem.
Forgetting to say how you would know it worked.

categories.title: Product Design
categories.summary: Can you turn a need into a concrete experience: flows, edge cases and the one screen that matters?
steps: Restate the job the user is hiring the product to do.
Walk the end-to-end journey, including the first-run and the failure path.
Sketch the key screen or interaction in words.
Call out accessibility, edge cases and abuse cases.
Cut to an MVP and say what you deferred.
pitfalls: Describing UI chrome instead of the interaction.
Ignoring the empty, error and slow states.

categories.title: Product Execution
categories.summary: Can you ship and run a product: diagnose metric movements, make launch calls, and keep a team moving?
steps: Check the data and the definition before the explanation.
Split internal causes (releases, bugs, logging) from external ones (seasonality, competitors, platforms).
Segment: platform, geography, cohort, surface, user type.
Form ranked hypotheses and the cheapest test for each.
Decide, communicate and set a follow-up.
pitfalls: Explaining a drop before confirming it is real.
Listing twenty hypotheses with no order.

categories.title: Product Strategy
categories.summary: Where should the product play, how will it win, and in what order?
steps: State the company's goal and the product's role in it.
Size the opportunity and the alternatives users have today.
Name the advantage you can build or use.
Choose a sequence of bets; each unlocks the next.
Say what you would watch to know the strategy is wrong.
pitfalls: A list of features called a strategy.

categories.title: Product Metrics & Analytics
categories.summary: Can you define success, choose a north-star and guardrails, and read the numbers honestly?
steps: Start from the product's purpose, not from available data.
Pick one primary metric that moves when users get value.
Add guardrails for the harm the primary metric could hide.
Define each metric precisely (numerator, denominator, window).
Say how you would detect gaming or measurement error.
pitfalls: Vanity metrics (sign-ups, page views) as goals.

categories.title: Prioritisation (RICE · ICE · MoSCoW)
categories.summary: Can you choose what not to do and defend it?
steps: Agree the goal the backlog serves.
Score with a framework the room accepts — RICE (reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort), ICE, or MoSCoW for scope.
Sanity-check the scores against strategy and dependencies.
Make the cut explicit and say what you are giving up.
Set when you will revisit.
pitfalls: Treating framework scores as truth rather than a conversation tool.
Ignoring confidence: big impact with no evidence.

categories.title: Roadmapping & Trade-offs
categories.summary: Can you turn strategy into a sequenced plan that survives contact with reality?
steps: Group work into outcomes, not features.
Sequence by dependency, learning value and risk.
Commit near-term, keep later horizons as bets.
Show what was traded off and why.
Explain how the roadmap changes when evidence changes.
pitfalls: A dated feature list sold as a promise.
No room for learning or maintenance.

categories.title: Experimentation & A/B Testing
categories.summary: Can you design a test whose result you would trust, and read it correctly?
steps: Write the hypothesis and the decision it will drive.
Pick the unit of randomisation and the primary metric.
Estimate sample size and duration (power, minimum detectable effect).
Name guardrails, novelty effects and network effects.
Pre-commit to the decision rule.
pitfalls: Peeking and stopping on the first significant day.
Randomising by user when the effect spreads between users.

categories.title: Stakeholder Management
categories.summary: Can you get people with different incentives to one decision?
steps: Map who decides, who is consulted, who is affected.
Understand each party's incentive and constraint.
Find the shared goal; frame options against it.
Escalate with options and a recommendation, not a complaint.
Close the loop in writing.
pitfalls: Escalating too early or too late.
Winning the argument and losing the relationship.

categories.title: Behavioural & Leadership
categories.summary: What have you actually done, how did you decide, and what did you learn?
steps: Pick a story where you made a decision that mattered.
Use a structure such as STAR (situation, task, action, result).
Spend most of the time on your actions and reasoning.
Quantify the result honestly, including partial failure.
End with what you would do differently.
pitfalls: 'We' all the way through — what did YOU do?
A story with no tension or trade-off.

categories.title: AI Product Strategy
categories.summary: Where does AI create defensible value, and where is it a costly feature nobody needs?
steps: Start from a user job, not from the model.
Ask whether AI is necessary, sufficient, or just novel.
Find the moat: proprietary data, workflow position, distribution, evaluation know-how.
Plan for model commoditisation and price drops.
Sequence: assist → automate → autonomous, as trust is earned.
pitfalls: Assuming today's model costs and limits are permanent.

categories.title: Generative AI & LLM Fundamentals
categories.summary: Do you understand how language models work well enough to make product calls?
steps: Explain tokens, context windows and next-token prediction in plain words.
Know what pre-training, fine-tuning and preference tuning change.
Know why outputs vary (sampling, temperature) and why models confabulate.
Connect each property to a product consequence.
pitfalls: Claiming a model 'knows' or 'looks up' facts.
Hand-waving about 'training it on our data'.

categories.title: RAG Architecture & Trade-offs
categories.summary: Can you ground a model in your own content, and know when that is the right tool?
steps: Describe the pipeline: ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → rerank → generate with citations.
Name the failure points: stale index, bad chunking, missed retrieval, unfaithful generation.
Compare with long-context prompting and fine-tuning.
Measure retrieval and answer quality separately.
Respect permissions: retrieval must not leak documents a user cannot see.
pitfalls: Blaming the model for retrieval failures.
Forgetting access control in the index.

categories.title: Agentic AI Use Cases
categories.summary: When should software plan and act on its own, and how do you keep it safe and useful?
steps: Pick tasks with clear goals, checkable outcomes and reversible actions.
Define the tools, their permissions and their blast radius.
Design checkpoints: what the agent may do alone, what needs approval.
Measure task success, intervention rate, cost per task and incidents.
Plan for loops, partial failure and prompt injection.
pitfalls: Giving an agent irreversible actions on day one.
Measuring 'steps taken' instead of tasks completed correctly.

categories.title: Prompt Engineering & Evaluation
categories.summary: Can you make model behaviour measurable and improve it deliberately?
steps: Write a golden set of real, representative cases with expected properties.
Define graders: exact checks, rubric-based human review, model-graded with calibration.
Change one thing at a time; compare against the baseline.
Track regressions on every prompt or model change.
Sample production traffic to keep the set honest.
pitfalls: Model-graded evals never checked against humans.

categories.title: Model Selection: Proprietary vs Open-Weight
categories.summary: Which model, hosted where, for which job?
steps: Write the requirements: quality bar, latency, cost per task, data residency, customisation.
Evaluate candidates on YOUR eval set, not public leaderboards.
Weigh proprietary APIs (capability, speed to ship) against open-weight (control, cost at scale, on-prem).
Design for switching: abstraction layer, portable evals.
Revisit as prices and capabilities change.
pitfalls: Ignoring the operational cost of self-hosting.

categories.title: AI Product Metrics & Quality
categories.summary: How do you know an AI feature is good, and getting better?
steps: Separate model quality (accuracy, faithfulness) from product value (task success, retention).
Add trust signals: corrections, overrides, escalations, thumbs-down with reasons.
Track cost and latency per successful task.
Segment by intent and difficulty; averages hide failures.
Close the loop: failures feed the eval set.

categories.title: Hallucinations, Reliability, Privacy & Safety
categories.summary: What can go wrong, for whom, and what stops it?
steps: List harms by severity: wrong facts, unsafe advice, data leakage, misuse, unfair outcomes.
Mitigate in layers: grounding, refusal policy, output checks, human review, rate limits.
Handle personal data: minimisation, retention, consent, no training without permission.
Red-team before launch; monitor after.
Set a launch bar and an owner who can stop the launch.
pitfalls: No plan for the first public failure.

categories.title: Cost, Latency & Accuracy Trade-offs
categories.summary: Can you make an AI product affordable and fast without making it wrong?
steps: Measure cost and latency per completed task, not per call.
Route: small model first, larger model when needed.
Cache, batch, trim context, stream partial results.
Decide where accuracy is non-negotiable and where 'good enough' is fine.
Model unit economics at 10× usage.
pitfalls: Optimising cost per token while tasks need three retries.

categories.title: Human-in-the-Loop Design
categories.summary: Where do people stay in control, and how does the system learn from them?
steps: Place review where errors are costly or irreversible.
Make review fast: show sources, confidence and the diff.
Avoid rubber-stamping: sample, rotate, measure reviewer agreement.
Feed corrections back into evaluation.
Plan the path from review-everything to review-exceptions.
pitfalls: Humans as a liability shield rather than a control.
Reviewers with no time and no context.

categories.title: AI Monetisation & ROI
categories.summary: Who pays, for what, and does it make money after inference costs?
steps: Tie value to an outcome the buyer measures (time saved, tickets resolved).
Pick a model: bundled, add-on seat, usage-based, outcome-based.
Compute gross margin with realistic usage and retries.
Plan for falling model prices and competitor bundling.
Prove ROI with a before/after or a holdout.
pitfalls: Unlimited usage on a flat price.

categories.title: The ML Product Lifecycle
categories.summary: Predictive models (ranking, fraud, forecasting) have their own lifecycle: labels, training, offline and online evaluation, drift and retraining.
steps: Define the prediction and the decision it drives.
Find labels: where truth comes from, how late, how biased.
Evaluate offline (precision, recall, calibration) then online (the product metric).
Plan monitoring for drift and feedback loops.
Decide the retraining cadence and the rollback path.
pitfalls: Optimising offline accuracy that does not move the product metric.
Feedback loops: the model shapes the data it later learns from.

categories.title: Program Planning & Execution
categories.summary: Can you turn a goal into a plan many teams can execute?
steps: Define the outcome, scope and the definition of done.
Break down into workstreams with owners.
Build the dependency graph and milestones.
Set the operating cadence: reviews, status, decision log.
Re-plan deliberately when facts change.
pitfalls: Status meetings that never decide anything.

categories.title: Cross-functional Dependency Management
categories.summary: Can you get teams with their own roadmaps to deliver what your program needs, when it needs it?
steps: Find dependencies early: interfaces, shared services, approvals.
Make each one explicit: what, who, by when, how verified.
Negotiate using the other team's goals, not only yours.
Track leading indicators, not just due dates.
Escalate early with options.
pitfalls: Discovering a dependency at integration time.
Assuming 'they said yes' means it is scheduled.

categories.title: Engineering Architecture Literacy
categories.summary: Can you follow a system design and see where the program risk lives?
steps: Draw the components, data flows and interfaces.
Identify state, ownership and failure domains.
Spot migration risks: dual writes, backfills, cutovers.
Ask about scale, consistency and rollback.
Translate technical risk into schedule and scope risk.
pitfalls: Nodding along without understanding the critical interface.

categories.title: Distributed Systems Fundamentals
categories.summary: Do you know why systems at scale fail in the ways they do?
steps: Explain latency, throughput, replication and partitioning in plain terms.
Know consistency trade-offs and idempotency.
Know common failure modes: cascading failure, hot keys, retries storms.
Know how rollouts reduce risk: canaries, feature flags, staged regions.
Connect each to program decisions.

categories.title: Risk Assessment & Mitigation
categories.summary: Can you see trouble coming and buy time against it?
steps: List risks by likelihood × impact.
Assign an owner, a mitigation and a trigger for each.
Retire the largest unknowns first (spikes, prototypes).
Keep contingency in the schedule where risk concentrates.
Review the register on a cadence.

categories.title: Critical-Path Analysis
categories.summary: Which chain of work sets the date, and how do you shorten it?
steps: Lay out tasks with durations and dependencies.
Find the longest dependent chain: that is the date.
Shorten it: parallelise, de-scope, add capacity where it helps, remove waits.
Watch near-critical paths; they become critical.
Re-run when estimates change.
pitfalls: Adding people to a late task that cannot be split.

categories.title: Delivery Forecasts & Milestones
categories.summary: Can you give a date you believe and explain its uncertainty?
steps: Forecast from evidence: throughput history, not wishes.
Give a range with a confidence level.
Set milestones that prove progress (integrated, tested), not activity.
Update the forecast when evidence changes, and say why.
Separate commitment from target.

categories.title: Incident Escalation
categories.summary: When something breaks, can you coordinate a calm, fast, honest response?
steps: Declare early; set severity and roles (incident lead, comms, scribe).
Stabilise first, then diagnose.
Communicate on a fixed cadence to the right audiences.
Decide on rollbacks and customer impact quickly.
Run a blameless review with owned actions.
pitfalls: Too many people debugging, nobody communicating.

categories.title: Technical Trade-offs
categories.summary: Can you help engineers and leaders choose between imperfect options?
steps: Frame the decision and its deadline.
List options with cost, risk, reversibility and time.
Bring the data the decision needs.
Recommend, record the decision and the dissent.
Name the trigger to revisit.
pitfalls: Deciding for engineering instead of with them.

categories.title: Executive Communication
categories.summary: Can you tell leaders the truth about a program in two minutes?
steps: Lead with status and the decision you need.
Show the trend, not just the state.
Name the top risks and what you are doing.
Ask for specific help.
Keep the same format every time.
pitfalls: Watermelon status: green outside, red inside.

categories.title: Program Health Metrics
categories.summary: How do you know a program is on track before the date slips?
steps: Pick leading indicators: milestone burn, dependency health, open risks, scope change.
Add quality signals: defect trend, test pass rate, error budgets.
Track team health: on-call load, attrition risk.
Define thresholds for yellow and red in advance.
Report trends and act on thresholds.

categories.title: Technical Product Sense
categories.summary: For a technical product, can you find the developer's real problem and shape the product around it?
steps: Identify the developer persona and their workflow.
Find the friction: setup, integration, debugging, scale, cost.
Define the product surface (API, SDK, console, CLI) and its contract.
Plan adoption: docs, samples, migration path.
Define success in developer outcomes.
pitfalls: Designing the API you would like to build, not the one developers need.

categories.title: API & Platform Design
categories.summary: Can you design an interface other teams will build on for years?
steps: Model the resources and operations users need.
Choose consistent naming, pagination, errors and idempotency.
Plan versioning and deprecation from day one.
Define limits, quotas and SLAs.
Write the getting-started path before the reference.
pitfalls: Leaking internal models into the API.
Breaking changes without a migration path.

categories.title: Requirements & Specs with Engineering
categories.summary: Can you write a spec engineers trust and use?
steps: State the problem, users, goals and non-goals.
Write requirements as behaviours and constraints, not designs.
Agree success metrics and launch criteria.
List open questions and who answers them.
Review with engineering early; let design emerge with them.
pitfalls: Non-goals left implicit, so scope creeps.

categories.title: Developer & Platform Metrics
categories.summary: How do you measure a product whose users are developers?
steps: Time to first successful call / first value.
Activation and retention of integrations, not sign-ups.
Reliability: error rates, latency, SLA attainment.
Support load and documentation success.
Revenue or internal cost saved, where relevant.
pitfalls: Ignoring the long tail of failed integrations.

categories.title: Build vs Buy vs Partner
categories.summary: Should we build it, buy it, or rely on someone else's?
steps: Is it core to our advantage?
Compare total cost of ownership over three years.
Assess time to market and the opportunity cost of the team.
Assess lock-in, security, compliance and exit paths.
Decide, and set the review trigger.
pitfalls: Comparing licence price to engineer salary only.

categories.title: Product Vision
categories.summary: Can you describe a future worth building toward that people will organise around?
steps: Describe the customer's world in three to five years.
Name the big insight competitors are missing.
Connect vision to near-term bets.
Make it memorable and testable.
Explain how it changes what teams do on Monday.
pitfalls: A vision that is a roadmap in disguise.

categories.title: Portfolio Strategy
categories.summary: How do you allocate people and money across several products and bets?
steps: Classify investments: core, adjacent, transformational.
Allocate deliberately (for example 70/20/10) and say why.
Define kill and scale criteria for bets.
Rebalance on evidence, on a cadence.
Communicate the allocation and its reasons.
pitfalls: No criteria to stop a bet.

categories.title: Organisation Design & Leadership
categories.summary: How should product teams be shaped, run and developed?
steps: Align team boundaries with customer problems and architecture.
Set clear ownership and decision rights.
Design the operating rhythm: planning, reviews, metrics.
Grow leaders; avoid becoming the bottleneck.
Change structure deliberately and explain why.
pitfalls: Reorgs as a substitute for strategy.
Managing PMs by reviewing their documents only.

categories.title: Hiring, Coaching & Performance
categories.summary: Can you build and grow a strong product team?
steps: Define the bar for each level with examples.
Hire for the gaps the strategy needs.
Coach with specific, timely feedback.
Handle under-performance fairly and promptly.
Create growth paths for ICs and managers.

categories.title: Executive & Board Communication
categories.summary: Can you persuade leaders and represent the product to the company's top decision-makers?
steps: Lead with the decision or the insight.
Frame in company terms: growth, margin, risk.
Show options and your recommendation.
Anticipate the hardest question.
Follow up in writing.
pitfalls: Defending your team instead of informing the decision.

categories.title: Metrics Systems for an Organisation
categories.summary: How do you design the goals and metrics many teams use to steer?
steps: Build a metric tree from company goal to team inputs.
Give each team metrics it can move.
Avoid metrics that make teams compete destructively.
Review on a cadence; retire stale metrics.
Protect the definitions.
pitfalls: Each team optimising its own metric against the user.

categories.title: Influence Without Authority
categories.summary: Can you change direction across teams you do not manage?
steps: Understand the other teams' goals.
Build the case with evidence and their language.
Start with a small, visible win.
Bring allies; make it their idea too.
Escalate as a last resort, with options.

categories.title: Data as a Product
categories.summary: Can you run a dataset or data platform like a product with users, quality bars and a roadmap?
steps: Identify data consumers and the decisions they make.
Define the product: datasets, contracts, freshness, access.
Set quality SLAs and owners.
Measure adoption and trust, not table counts.
Plan the roadmap with consumers.

categories.title: Data Quality & Trust
categories.summary: How do you make numbers that people can rely on?
steps: Define quality dimensions: freshness, completeness, accuracy, consistency.
Use data contracts at producer boundaries.
Monitor and alert on tests and anomalies.
Make incidents visible to consumers.
Fix root causes upstream.
pitfalls: Testing only at the end of the pipeline.

categories.title: Data Governance, Privacy & Access
categories.summary: Who may see which data, for what purpose, and how is that enforced?
steps: Classify data by sensitivity.
Define purpose-based access and least privilege.
Handle retention, deletion and consent.
Audit access and lineage.
Make the compliant path the easy path.

categories.title: Data Stakeholders & Prioritisation
categories.summary: Many teams want data work; how do you choose?
steps: Tie requests to decisions and their value.
Prefer platform capabilities over one-off tables.
Make capacity and trade-offs visible.
Agree priorities in a shared forum.
Say no with a reason and an alternative.
pitfalls: Building bespoke pipelines for every team.

categories.title: Platform Strategy
categories.summary: What should be shared infrastructure, and how do you get teams to use it?
steps: Find the repeated problem across teams.
Decide the platform's scope and what stays with teams.
Design for self-service.
Plan adoption: migration support, incentives, deprecation.
Measure platform value in teams' outcomes.
pitfalls: Building a platform before there are two customers.
Mandating adoption of an unready platform.

categories.title: Internal Customers
categories.summary: How do you discover and serve users who are other teams?
steps: Interview teams like external customers.
Segment them by need and maturity.
Publish a roadmap and an intake process.
Offer clear SLAs and support channels.
Measure satisfaction and time saved.
pitfalls: Assuming internal users have to use you.

categories.title: Migrations & Deprecations
categories.summary: How do you move many teams from an old system to a new one?
steps: Make the new path clearly better.
Provide tooling and do the first migrations yourself.
Set dates with escalation paths.
Track migration progress publicly.
Turn off the old system — really.

categories.title: Growth Loops & Models
categories.summary: How does the product acquire, activate and retain users, and how does each feed the next?
steps: Draw the loop: how new users create more new users or value.
Model the funnel and its conversion rates.
Find the constraint step.
Prioritise experiments on the constraint.
Check that growth is healthy (quality, retention).
pitfalls: Optimising a step that is not the constraint.

categories.title: Funnel & Activation Analysis
categories.summary: Where do users drop off, and why?
steps: Define each step and the activation moment ('aha').
Measure conversion by cohort and channel.
Watch real sessions; talk to drop-offs.
Form hypotheses and test the biggest leak.
Track time-to-value.
pitfalls: Fixing UI when the problem is the promise.

categories.title: Growth Experimentation
categories.summary: Can you run many fast experiments without fooling yourself or harming users?
steps: Keep a prioritised experiment backlog.
Size tests for the effect you can detect.
Watch guardrails: retention, complaints, revenue quality.
Avoid dark patterns.
Share learnings, including null results.

categories.title: Monetisation & Pricing
categories.summary: How should the product make money, and at what price?
steps: Find the value metric customers care about.
Choose packaging: tiers, add-ons, usage.
Test willingness to pay.
Model revenue, conversion and churn effects.
Grandfather and communicate changes carefully.

categories.title: Retention & Engagement
categories.summary: Why do users stay, why do they leave, and what brings them back?
steps: Plot retention curves by cohort; find where they flatten.
Identify behaviours that predict retention.
Distinguish habit, value and lock-in.
Design re-engagement that respects users.
Measure resurrected users separately.

categories.title: Metric Design
categories.summary: Can you turn a fuzzy question into a precise, robust metric?
steps: Write the question the metric answers.
Define numerator, denominator, unit and window.
Handle edge cases: bots, test accounts, time zones, late data.
Check sensitivity and gaming.
Document it where people will find it.
pitfalls: Ratio metrics with a moving denominator.

categories.title: SQL & Data Analysis
categories.summary: Can you get the right answer out of raw tables, correctly?
steps: Understand the grain of every table.
Join deliberately; check row counts after each join.
Handle NULLs, duplicates and time zones.
Validate against a known number.
Explain the result in one sentence.
pitfalls: Filtering after an outer join and losing rows.

categories.title: Experiment Analysis
categories.summary: Can you read an A/B test honestly?
steps: Check sample ratio and assignment first.
Read the primary metric with its confidence interval.
Check guardrails and segments (pre-registered ones).
Watch for novelty, interference and multiple comparisons.
Recommend a decision and its risk.
pitfalls: Hunting through segments for a win.

categories.title: Root-Cause Analysis
categories.summary: A metric moved. What happened?
steps: Confirm the change is real (definition, logging, pipeline).
Find when it started and how fast.
Decompose: segments, funnel steps, mix vs rate.
Match to events: releases, campaigns, outages, seasonality.
Test the leading hypothesis with data.
pitfalls: Stopping at the first plausible story.

categories.title: Communicating Insights
categories.summary: Can you make an analysis change a decision?
steps: Lead with the answer and the recommendation.
Show the one chart that proves it.
State confidence and caveats plainly.
Offer the next question to answer.
Tailor depth to the audience.
pitfalls: A deck of twenty charts and no point.

categories.title: Positioning
categories.summary: For whom is this product the best choice, instead of what, and why?
steps: Identify the best-fit customer.
Name the real alternatives (including doing nothing).
List the unique attributes and the value they enable.
Choose the market category frame.
Test the positioning with customers and sales.

categories.title: Go-to-Market & Launch
categories.summary: Can you take a product to market so the right people hear, try and buy it?
steps: Set launch goals and tier the launch by importance.
Define audience, message and channels.
Enable sales, support and partners.
Coordinate timing and readiness.
Measure and iterate after launch.

categories.title: Messaging & Narrative
categories.summary: Can you write the words that make the value land?
steps: Start from the customer's problem in their words.
Build a message hierarchy: headline, three pillars, proof.
Adapt by audience: buyer, user, technical evaluator.
Test messages (interviews, ads, win/loss).
Keep it consistent across channels.

categories.title: Market & Competitive Research
categories.summary: What do you know about buyers and competitors, and how do you know it?
steps: Define the research question.
Mix methods: interviews, win/loss, surveys, usage data.
Map competitors by segment and strength.
Turn findings into implications.
Keep the research current.

categories.title: GTM Metrics & Sales Enablement
categories.summary: How do you know marketing and sales are working together, and working?
steps: Track pipeline created and influenced, win rate, cycle time.
Measure adoption of enablement assets.
Run win/loss analysis.
Attribute carefully; avoid double counting.
Feed findings back to product.

categories.title: Operating Cadence
categories.summary: What rhythm keeps a product organisation aligned without drowning it in meetings?
steps: Map decisions to forums: planning, reviews, launches.
Set the cadence for each and its inputs.
Standardise artefacts (one-pagers, review templates).
Measure the cost in time and remove what does not decide.
Revisit each half.

categories.title: Product Tooling & Systems
categories.summary: Which tools and data make PMs and teams faster?
steps: Find the workflow pain first.
Choose tools that integrate with how teams work.
Define a single source of truth for roadmaps and feedback.
Drive adoption with templates and training.
Measure time saved.
pitfalls: Buying a tool to fix a process problem.

categories.title: Customer Insights Operations
categories.summary: How do customer signals reach the people who decide?
steps: Collect feedback from support, sales, research and usage.
Tag and route it consistently.
Quantify themes by customer value and frequency.
Report themes to product reviews.
Close the loop with customers.

categories.title: Launch Process & Readiness
categories.summary: How does a product org ship reliably?
steps: Define launch tiers and their checklists.
Gate on readiness: quality, support, legal, docs.
Coordinate calendars across teams.
Run go/no-go with clear owners.
Review launches and improve the process.
pitfalls: A checklist so long nobody follows it.

categories.title: Product Org Health Metrics
categories.summary: How do you measure whether the product organisation is working well?
steps: Measure flow: cycle time from idea to launch.
Measure outcomes: goal attainment.
Measure quality: incidents, rollbacks.
Measure people: engagement, attrition.
Act on trends, not single points.
pitfalls: Using the metrics to rank PMs.

categories.title: Market Sizing
categories.summary: How big is the opportunity, really?
steps: Define the market precisely.
Size top-down and bottom-up; compare.
State every assumption with its source or reasoning.
Sensitivity-test the biggest assumptions.
Convert to what we can serve and win.

categories.title: Competitive Strategy
categories.summary: How will competitors respond, and how do we stay ahead?
steps: Map competitors and their incentives.
Identify sources of advantage: scale, network, data, switching cost, brand.
Predict moves and counter-moves.
Choose where not to compete.
Watch signals.

categories.title: Business Cases
categories.summary: Should we invest, and how much?
steps: State the decision and alternatives.
Model revenue, cost and timing with ranges.
Include risks and strategic value.
Compute payback and sensitivity.
Recommend with conditions.

categories.title: Strategic Bets & Partnerships
categories.summary: Enter, partner, acquire, or wait?
steps: Define the strategic goal.
Compare build, partner, acquire, invest, wait.
Assess fit, cost, time and risk.
Define success milestones and exit criteria.
Plan integration or partnership governance.

categories.title: Strategy Communication
categories.summary: Can you turn analysis into a story leaders act on?
steps: Start with the recommendation.
Show the logic in three steps.
Make the trade-offs explicit.
Pre-wire key stakeholders.
Leave a written memo.
pitfalls: Analysis without a point of view.

dimensions.name: Problem framing
dimensions.listens_for: Clarifies the goal, the user and the constraint before solving; states assumptions out loud.
anchors: Jumps to a solution; the problem is never defined.
Asks some questions but does not use the answers.
Defines goal, user and scope, and states the key assumptions.
Reframes the problem usefully and shows why that framing beats the obvious one.

dimensions.name: Structured thinking
dimensions.listens_for: An answer the listener can follow: a stated plan, mutually exclusive buckets, a clear order.
anchors: Ideas arrive in no order; hard to follow.
A structure is announced but not kept.
A clear structure is stated and followed.
The structure itself does work: it exposes what matters and what can be ignored.

dimensions.name: User insight
dimensions.listens_for: Specific users with specific needs and contexts, not 'users' in general.
anchors: Talks about features, not people.
Names a user segment but not its needs.
Picks a segment deliberately and grounds needs in its context.
Finds a non-obvious need and shows why it matters most.

dimensions.name: Business judgment
dimensions.listens_for: Connects the answer to value: revenue, cost, strategic position, risk.
anchors: No link to the business.
Mentions value in passing.
Ties the recommendation to a business outcome with rough size.
Weighs value against cost and strategic fit, and says what would change the call.

dimensions.name: Metrics
dimensions.listens_for: A primary metric that matches the goal, guardrails that catch harm, and how each is measured.
anchors: No metrics, or vanity metrics only.
Lists metrics without choosing.
Chooses a primary metric with guardrails and explains why.
Anticipates how the metric could mislead and designs against it.

dimensions.name: Prioritisation
dimensions.listens_for: Explicit choices with a stated basis, including what is NOT done.
anchors: Everything is a priority.
Ranks without a basis.
Ranks with a stated framework or criteria.
Makes a hard cut, explains the cost of it, and when to revisit.

dimensions.name: Trade-off reasoning
dimensions.listens_for: Names the options, what each gives up, and the reason for the choice.
anchors: One option, no alternatives.
Alternatives named, costs not.
Compares options on explicit criteria and chooses.
Finds the option that changes the trade-off, or the reversible path.

dimensions.name: Execution
dimensions.listens_for: A plan that could actually ship: sequencing, owners, milestones, what happens when it slips.
anchors: No plan.
A list of steps without order or owners.
Sequenced plan with milestones and owners.
Plan with explicit risk buffers, decision points and a fallback.

dimensions.name: Technical depth
dimensions.listens_for: Understands how the system works well enough to make sound decisions with engineers.
anchors: Avoids or misstates the technology.
Uses the right terms shallowly.
Explains the mechanism and its implications for the product.
Spots the technical constraint that changes the product decision.

dimensions.name: AI literacy
dimensions.listens_for: Knows what models can and cannot do, how they fail, and how quality is measured.
anchors: Treats the model as magic.
Knows the vocabulary, not the failure modes.
Explains capabilities, failure modes and evaluation in product terms.
Designs the product around the model's failure modes.

dimensions.name: Safety & trust
dimensions.listens_for: Anticipates harm to users and third parties; privacy, misuse and reliability are designed in, not bolted on.
anchors: No mention of harm or misuse.
Mentions risk generically.
Identifies concrete risks with mitigations and a launch bar.
Sets a launch bar the team can test, and says who decides when it is not met.

dimensions.name: Risk management
dimensions.listens_for: Finds risks early, sizes them, and owns mitigations and triggers.
anchors: Risks discovered when they happen.
Lists risks without likelihood or impact.
A risk register with owners, mitigations and triggers.
Retires the biggest risk first and buys options against the rest.

dimensions.name: Stakeholder management
dimensions.listens_for: Knows who must agree, what each cares about, and how disagreement gets resolved.
anchors: Stakeholders appear as obstacles.
Names stakeholders, not their incentives.
Maps incentives and plans alignment and escalation.
Turns a conflict into a decision the parties can live with, at the right level.

dimensions.name: Communication
dimensions.listens_for: Clear, concise, audience-aware; leads with the answer.
anchors: Rambling; the point is lost.
Clear in parts, buries the lead.
Leads with the answer, then supports it.
Adapts depth to the audience and checks understanding.

dimensions.name: Leadership
dimensions.listens_for: Ownership, judgment under ambiguity, developing others, and learning from failure.
anchors: Credits or blames others; no ownership.
Owns the work, not the outcome.
Owns the outcome, explains decisions and what they learned.
Raised the bar for others and changed how the team works.

dimensions.name: Analytical rigour
dimensions.listens_for: Checks the data before trusting it; separates correlation, causation and noise.
anchors: Takes numbers at face value.
Asks about data quality without acting on it.
Validates data, segments sensibly, tests hypotheses in order.
Designs the analysis so its answer is hard to fool.

dimensions.name: Strategic thinking
dimensions.listens_for: Where to play and how to win: market, advantage, sequencing, and what competitors will do.
anchors: Tactics only.
A goal without a path.
A coherent strategy with a reasoned sequence.
A strategy that builds advantage over time and names what would falsify it.

dimensions.name: Market & message
dimensions.listens_for: Understands the buyer, the alternatives and the words that make the value land.
anchors: Product features instead of buyer value.
Generic positioning.
Positioning grounded in buyer, alternative and proof.
Positioning that forces a sharp choice and is testable in market.

tracks.title: AI Product Management
tracks.summary: Product management for AI, generative AI, ML, AI platforms and agents: where AI earns its place, how it fails, how quality is measured and how it is shipped safely and profitably.
tracks.tests: Whether you can make sound product decisions about systems that are probabilistic, expensive to run and capable of harm — and explain those decisions to engineers, researchers and executives.

rounds.title: AI Product Strategy
rounds.focus: Where AI creates defensible value, and how it pays for itself.

rounds.title: Technical AI Literacy
rounds.focus: How the system works and what that means for the product.

rounds.title: AI Evaluation and Safety
rounds.focus: Measuring quality, finding failure modes, and setting a launch bar.

rounds.title: Product Execution
rounds.focus: Turning an AI idea into a shippable MVP with the right controls.

rounds.title: Cross-functional Leadership
rounds.focus: Working between research, engineering, legal and sales when quality is uncertain.

tracks.title: Data Product Management
tracks.summary: Product management where the product is data: datasets, metrics layers, data platforms and the trust people place in the numbers.
tracks.tests: Whether you can treat data as a product with users and quality bars, govern it responsibly, and choose between many teams' requests.

rounds.title: Data Product Sense
rounds.focus: Who uses the data, for what decision, and what product serves them.

rounds.title: Data Quality and Trust
rounds.focus: Making numbers people can rely on.

rounds.title: Governance and Privacy
rounds.focus: Access, purpose and personal data — designed in, not added later.

rounds.title: Prioritisation Across Teams
rounds.focus: Choosing between many teams' data requests.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Ownership when the numbers are wrong.

tracks.title: Growth Product Management
tracks.summary: Product management for acquisition, activation, retention and monetisation: growth models, funnels, fast experiments and pricing.
tracks.tests: Whether you can find the constraint in a growth model, run many honest experiments, and grow without harming users or long-term retention.

rounds.title: Growth Model
rounds.focus: How the product grows, and which step is the constraint.

rounds.title: Funnel and Activation
rounds.focus: Where users drop off, and why.

rounds.title: Experimentation
rounds.focus: Fast tests you would trust, with guardrails.

rounds.title: Retention and Monetisation
rounds.focus: Keeping users, and charging them fairly.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Judgment about growth that would hurt users.

tracks.title: Platform Product Management
tracks.summary: Product management for platforms whose customers are other teams or developers: what to share, how to get it adopted, and how to move everyone off the old way.
tracks.tests: Whether you can find the repeated problem worth a platform, serve internal customers who have choices, and run adoption and migrations without mandates you cannot back.

rounds.title: Platform Strategy
rounds.focus: What should be shared infrastructure, and what should stay with teams.

rounds.title: Internal Customers
rounds.focus: Discovering and serving users who are other teams.

rounds.title: Adoption and Platform Metrics
rounds.focus: Measuring platform value in the outcomes of the teams that use it.

rounds.title: Migrations
rounds.focus: Moving many teams to a new platform — and turning the old one off.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Influencing teams that do not have to use you.

tracks.title: Product Management
tracks.summary: The core product management interview: product sense and design, execution, strategy and prioritisation, metrics and experiments, and leadership.
tracks.tests: Whether you can find the right problem, choose what to build, ship it, measure it honestly and bring people with you.

rounds.title: Product Sense
rounds.focus: Problem framing, user insight and a clear, testable product idea.

rounds.title: Product Execution
rounds.focus: Diagnosing a metric change and making a launch call under uncertainty.

rounds.title: Strategy and Prioritisation
rounds.focus: Where to play, what to build first, and what you will not do.

rounds.title: Analytics and Experimentation
rounds.focus: Choosing metrics that cannot fool you and tests you would trust.

rounds.title: Leadership and Behavioural
rounds.focus: Ownership, judgment and how you work with people.

tracks.title: Senior Product Leadership
tracks.summary: For Group PMs, Principal PMs and Directors of Product: vision, portfolio choices, organisation design, talent, executive communication and goal systems.
tracks.tests: Whether you can set direction for many teams, allocate people and money, build a strong product organisation and be trusted by the executive team.

rounds.title: Vision and Portfolio Strategy
rounds.focus: A direction many teams can organise around, and the allocation that funds it.

rounds.title: Organisation and Talent
rounds.focus: Team shapes, decision rights and growing product leaders.

rounds.title: Executive Communication
rounds.focus: Earning trust from the executive team and the board.

rounds.title: Goals and Operating System
rounds.focus: Metric trees and goals that make teams pull in the same direction.

rounds.title: Influence and Leadership
rounds.focus: Changing direction across teams you do not manage.

tracks.title: Product Marketing
tracks.summary: For product marketing managers: positioning, messaging, launches, market research and the metrics that connect marketing to revenue.
tracks.tests: Whether you understand the buyer and the alternatives, can find the words that make the value land, and can take a product to market so the right people hear, try and buy it.

rounds.title: Positioning
rounds.focus: For whom this product is the best choice, instead of what, and why.

rounds.title: Messaging
rounds.focus: Words that land with buyers, users and technical evaluators.

rounds.title: Launch Plan
rounds.focus: Taking a product to market, with sales ready on day one.

rounds.title: Research and GTM Metrics
rounds.focus: What you know about buyers, and whether go-to-market is working.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Working between product and sales.

tracks.title: Product Analytics
tracks.summary: For product analysts: designing metrics, getting correct answers from raw data, reading experiments honestly, finding why a number moved and making the answer change a decision.
tracks.tests: Whether your numbers are right, whether you can tell signal from noise, and whether a product team acts on what you find.

rounds.title: Metric Design
rounds.focus: Turning a fuzzy question into a precise, robust metric.

rounds.title: SQL and Data
rounds.focus: Grain, joins and the mistakes that double a number. Practise the executable SQL in the Question Bank too.

rounds.title: Experiment Analysis
rounds.focus: Reading an A/B test without fooling yourself.

rounds.title: Root-Cause Analysis
rounds.focus: A metric moved; find out why, in order.

rounds.title: Communicating Insight
rounds.focus: Making an analysis change a decision.

studio_links: The Revenue Problem (two definitions of revenue)

tracks.title: Product Operations
tracks.summary: For product operations managers: the operating cadence of a product organisation, its tools and data, customer-insight flow, launch process and the health of the organisation.
tracks.tests: Whether you can make a product organisation faster and better informed without burying it in process.

rounds.title: Operating Cadence
rounds.focus: Which forums decide what, and which ones to remove.

rounds.title: Customer Insights
rounds.focus: Getting customer signal to the people who decide.

rounds.title: Launch Process
rounds.focus: Shipping reliably across many teams.

rounds.title: Tools and Org Health
rounds.focus: Tools that help, and measures of whether the organisation works.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Changing how people work.

tracks.title: Product Strategy
tracks.summary: For product strategy managers: sizing markets, competitive strategy, business cases, strategic bets and partnerships, and turning analysis into a decision.
tracks.tests: Whether your analysis is sound and honest about uncertainty, and whether you can turn it into a clear recommendation that leaders act on.

rounds.title: Market Sizing
rounds.focus: How big the opportunity is, with every assumption visible.

rounds.title: Competitive Strategy
rounds.focus: Where to play, and how competitors will respond.

rounds.title: Business Case
rounds.focus: Should we invest, and how much?

rounds.title: Strategic Bets
rounds.focus: Build, partner, acquire or wait — and the memo that decides it.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: When the analysis said something unwelcome.

tracks.title: Technical Product Management
tracks.summary: Product management for technical products — APIs, SDKs, developer tools and platforms. You own what the product does and why, for users who are developers.
tracks.tests: Whether you can find a developer's real problem, design an interface they will build on for years, write specs engineers trust, and measure adoption honestly.

distinct_from.how: A Technical Product Manager owns WHAT a technical product does and WHY: the developer problem, the API contract, adoption and success metrics. A Technical Program Manager owns HOW and WHEN a multi-team effort is delivered. Technical PM interviews look like product interviews with deeper technical content; they do not test critical paths or program governance.

rounds.title: Technical Product Sense
rounds.focus: Finding the developer's real problem and shaping the product around it.

rounds.title: API and Platform Design
rounds.focus: An interface other teams can build on: resources, errors, versioning, limits.

rounds.title: Specs and Engineering Partnership
rounds.focus: Writing requirements, not designs; deciding what to build at all.

rounds.title: Adoption and Developer Metrics
rounds.focus: Measuring a product whose users are developers, and moving them to a new version.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Owning the what and the why while engineers own the how.

tracks.title: Technical Program Management
tracks.summary: Technical program management: planning and running multi-team engineering programs, managing dependencies and risk, understanding the architecture well enough to find the schedule risk, and telling leaders the truth.
tracks.tests: Whether you can deliver complex engineering work across teams you do not manage — and whether you understand the system well enough to know where it will go wrong.

distinct_from.how: A Technical Product Manager decides WHAT a technical product should do and WHY. A Technical Program Manager owns HOW and WHEN a multi-team engineering effort gets delivered. TPM interviews test planning, dependencies, critical paths, risk, escalation and executive communication — not product sense.

rounds.title: Technical Architecture
rounds.focus: Following a design closely enough to find where the program risk lives.

rounds.title: Program Execution
rounds.focus: Plans, critical paths, forecasts and health signals.

rounds.title: Risk and Dependency Management
rounds.focus: Seeing trouble early, and handling it calmly when it arrives.

rounds.title: Stakeholder Escalation
rounds.focus: Moving decisions to the right level with options and a recommendation.

rounds.title: Behavioural and Leadership
rounds.focus: Ownership, honesty about dates, and leading without authority.
